blocks.text: 1. Why You Need a Framework

Under interview pressure, you do not rise to the occasion, you fall to your preparation. A framework is a fixed sequence of steps you run every single time, so no nerves, no blank page, and no forgotten sections.

metadata.alt: The seven step framework, from clarifying to edge cases

blocks.text: The seven steps below fit any OOD problem, from a parking lot to a chess game. The order matters: each step produces exactly the input the next one needs, and interviewers recognise the discipline immediately.
Same seven steps, every problem, every time. The framework is the answer to "where do I start?"
blocks.content: Same seven steps, every problem, every time. The framework is the answer to "where do I start?"

blocks.text: 2. Step 1: Clarify Requirements
Spend the first five minutes asking questions, and say why: designing the wrong thing perfectly still fails. Your questions come from four buckets.

metadata.alt: The four buckets of clarifying questions

items: Actors: who uses this? A parking lot has drivers, gates, and admins; an ATM has customers, the bank, and operators
Features: which operations are in scope? Withdraw only, or deposits too? One floor or many?
Scale: one machine or a fleet? In memory or persistent? This decides how much you must design
Constraints: money handling, concurrency, limits, denominations, anything with sharp edges

blocks.text: Close the step by stating your assumptions out loud and writing the agreed feature list in a corner. That list is your contract; everything you build maps back to it.
3. Step 2: Identify the Core Objects

Underline the nouns in the requirements: each meaningful noun is a candidate class, and the verbs attached to it become its methods. This one technique reliably produces a solid first draft of the model.

metadata.alt: Nouns become classes, verbs become methods

blocks.text: From "vehicles park in spots and receive a ticket" you get Vehicle, ParkingSpot, and Ticket as classes, and park() as the operation that connects them. Filter out nouns that are just data, like colour, and merge synonyms, like car and vehicle.

items: Keep: nouns with behaviour or identity: Machine, Spot, Ticket, Account
Demote to fields: nouns that are pure data: price, plate number, expiry
Add the invisible ones: coordinators and policies the text never names, like Inventory or PricingStrategy

blocks.text: One class, one responsibility. If you cannot state a class job in one sentence, split it.
blocks.content: One class, one responsibility. If you cannot state a class job in one sentence, split it.

blocks.text: 4. Step 3: Define the Relationships
Now connect the objects, choosing the relationship deliberately. A simple decision path picks the right one every time.

metadata.alt: A decision path for choosing the relationship

items: Does the part die with the owner? Composition: a floor cannot outlive its lot
Held but independently alive? Aggregation: a spot holds a vehicle that will leave
Is it a kind of the other? Inheritance: a Car is a Vehicle
Just calls it? Association: the ATM uses the BankService

blocks.text: Say the relationship words out loud as you draw: "the lot composes floors, a spot aggregates its vehicle". This vocabulary is precisely what the interviewer is listening for in this step.
5. Step 4: Choose Patterns, With Reasons
Patterns are chosen by symptom, not by fashion. Look at what the problem keeps doing to you, and let that pick the pattern.

metadata.alt: Symptom to pattern: let the problem choose

items: Behaviour changes by mode: the same button does different things at different times. State pattern
A policy that will change: pricing, allocation, payment. Strategy behind an interface
A family of things to construct: vehicles, pieces, transactions. Factory method
Things reacting to events: displays, printers, alerts. Observer
A request that cascades: note denominations, approval levels. Chain of Responsibility

blocks.text: Then justify in one sentence: "I am using State because pressing A1 must behave differently before and after money is inserted." A pattern with a reason scores; a pattern without one costs.
6. Step 5: Sketch the UML
A small class diagram is your design made visible, and your checklist for the coding step. Draw boxes for the core classes, mark the interfaces, and arrow the relationships you chose.

metadata.alt: A minimal UML sketch for a coffee machine: context, state interface, and data

blocks.text: Keep it to six to ten classes. Attributes and methods only for the interesting ones, the context and the interfaces. The diagram is a conversation piece, not a specification: expect the interviewer to point at it and ask "why this arrow?"

items: Mark interfaces explicitly, they carry the design
Show the pattern in the picture: a state hierarchy hanging off the context is instantly readable
Leave room: you will add a class or two while coding, and that is normal

blocks.text: 7. Step 6: Write the Code, in the Right Order
blocks.content: 7. Step 6: Write the Code, in the Right Order

blocks.text: Code in dependency order, so everything you write compiles against what already exists. This ordering also front loads the easy wins while your nerves settle.

metadata.alt: Code in dependency order: enums to data to interfaces to core

blocks.text: Narrate as you type, and be honest about stubs: "I will stub the card gateway, the interface is what matters here." Prioritise the pattern carrying classes; if time runs short, describe the rest verbally over the UML.
8. Step 7: Edge Cases and Concurrency
Finish by attacking your own design before the interviewer does. Four questions expose almost every hole.

metadata.alt: The four questions that surface edge cases

items: Invalid input: unknown codes, negative amounts, expired cards. Reject with specific exceptions
Resource exhausted: lot full, out of stock, no change, no notes. Fail before any state changes
Two users, one resource: the last spot, the last item. Make the check and take one atomic step
Failure midway: power cut after payment. Order operations so every failure is free or reversible

blocks.text: The concurrency sentence that always lands: "the check and the update must be one atomic operation, and I lock the smallest thing possible, the spot, not the lot."
9. Managing the Clock
Forty five minutes disappears fast, so budget it like money. The framework maps onto the clock cleanly.

metadata.alt: A 45 minute budget across the seven steps

items: 0 to 5: clarify and write the agreed feature list
5 to 12: objects and relationships, spoken out loud
12 to 18: patterns with justification, and the UML sketch
18 to 38: code the core: enums, data, interfaces, the pattern classes, one happy path
38 to 45: edge cases, concurrency, and extensions you would build next

blocks.text: If you are still clarifying at minute ten, cut scope out loud and move. Controlling the clock is itself a scored skill.

blocks.text: 10. What to Say: The Scripts
A few rehearsed sentences carry you through the transitions, which is exactly where candidates freeze.

items: Opening: "Before designing, let me confirm the actors, the features in scope, and the constraints."
After clarifying: "I will design for these five features, in memory, single machine, and call out extensions at the end."
Introducing a pattern: "Behaviour changes by mode here, so each mode becomes a State class and the machine delegates."
Starting to code: "I will code in dependency order: enums, data classes, interfaces, then the core."
When stuck: "Let me re anchor on the requirement list", then pick the next feature and model it
Closing: "Given more time I would add persistence, the observer for the display, and tests for each state transition."

blocks.text: 11. A Worked Mini Example
Watch the framework compress a whole problem into four moves: design a coffee machine. This is the pace you want in a real interview.

metadata.alt: The framework applied end to end to a coffee machine in minutes

items: Clarify: coins only, three drinks, refunds allowed, one machine, ingredients tracked
Objects: CoffeeMachine, Recipe, Inventory, MachineState, Coin; recipes aggregate ingredient amounts
Relationships and pattern: machine composes inventory, delegates to MachineState: Idle and Paid; brewing checks the recipe against inventory
Code and edges: enums, Recipe, the two states, the machine facade; edge cases: insufficient ingredients, refund in Paid, exact change

blocks.text: Notice what carried over: the state machine from the vending problem, the recipe inventory idea from the coffee variation, and the same atomicity sentence for the last cup problem. The classics are transferable, and the framework is the carrier.
12. Key Takeaways
The framework is the product of every classic problem in this course, compressed into a repeatable script. Internalise it and no problem statement can blank you.

items: Clarify actors, features, scale, constraints, then state assumptions
Objects from the nouns, methods from the verbs, one responsibility each
Relationships chosen deliberately: composition, aggregation, inheritance, association
Patterns picked by symptom and justified in one sentence
UML small, interfaces marked, the pattern visible in the picture
Code in dependency order, narrating, honest about stubs
Edge cases and the atomicity sentence before the interviewer asks

blocks.text: Run the same seven steps every time. The problems change; your method never does.
blocks.content: Run the same seven steps every time. The problems change; your method never does.
